Importing the Forward Blocking Replication Pilot from JATOS

Source: vignettes/import-jatos-data.Rmd
import-jatos-data.Rmd

This copy was built without access to the data, so the code is shown but was not run. Prerequisites section below says how to run it.

This vignette imports the data of the pilot study fba-allergy-online-01 from the JATOS server that collected them and turns the import into a validated catlas_fba_rawdata bundle, including participant metadata, stimulus mappings and trial-level responses, together with a provenance record of where the data came from.

The pilot ran online between 9th and 26th June 2026, on JATOS at jatos.mindprobe.eu, using the three-stage allergy-prediction task from catlaslab. It was collected in four JATOS batches.

Prerequisites

  • A JATOS API token with access to the CATLAS study on jatos.mindprobe.eu, stored as mindprobe_catlas_token in your .Renviron (for instance via usethis::edit_r_environ())
  • {jatosR}, installed from GitHub via remotes::install_github("visionlabels/jatosR")
  • {jsonlite}
  • A private folder outside every repository, named by CATLAS_PRIVATE_DIR in your .Renviron, holding fba-allergy-online-01/meta-corrections.rds (see Corrected self-reports)

The raw data contain personal information, namely the participants’ age, sex and e-mail address, so the vignette saves its data bundles only when asked to and only to the private folder1. The import also reads from this folder, because the corrections of two untrue self-reports are personal data too. To import and save in a single step, run the following line from the package root:

rmarkdown::render(
  "vignettes/import-jatos-data.Rmd",
  params = list(save = TRUE)
)
library(catlasr)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(purrr)

1. Data download

The data are downloaded via jatosR, one batch at a time, implemented within the pull_jatos_batches() function. pull_jatos_batches() checks the connection and the proceeds to download all listed batches, naming any batch that could not be pulled. The batch IDs are later documented in the provenance record. The data bundle’s validator then uses them to check that every participant came from one of the listed batches and that each batch contributed at least one record.

jatos_url <- "https://jatos.mindprobe.eu"                # URL of the server that contains the data
study_id  <- "forward-blocking-replication-online-pilot" # Custom study ID, does not follow any structure rules
batch_ids <- c(30206L, 30275L, 30832L, 30829L)           # Batches that contain all the data we want to import
# The {catlasr} data pull yields a tibble with one row per JATOS study result,
# combining records from all batches. The download works via the {jatosR}
# workflow described at https://github.com/visionlabels/jatosR.git.
jatos_data <- pull_jatos_batches(
  url = jatos_url,
  batch_ids = batch_ids,
  token = Sys.getenv("mindprobe_catlas_token")
)

jatos_data_summary <- count(jatos_data, batch_id, study_state)
jatos_data_summary

Each row of jatos_data represents one JATOS study result, which correspond to a single person once opening the study link. Its id_sr is used as the participant identifier from now on.

2. Repair and parse

The experiment sends every jsPsych trial data to JATOS immediately after the trial is finished. JATOS stores these records back to back as {...}{...}{...} strings without the brackets and commas that would make the data a valid JSON array.2 The repair_jatos_json() function adds both missing parts:

# This code runs even without the data, so it names its package explicitly:
json_string <- catlasr::repair_jatos_json('{"trial_type":"consent","response":1}{"trial_type":"stimuli-map"}')
json_string
#> [1] "[{\"trial_type\":\"consent\",\"response\":1},{\"trial_type\":\"stimuli-map\"}]"

# The repaired data can then be parsed via the {jsonlite}:
jsonlite::parse_json(json_string, simplifyVector = TRUE)
#>    trial_type response
#> 1     consent        1
#> 2 stimuli-map       NA

parse_jatos_results() applies the repair to every result and then parses each result separately, so a single damaged result cannot stop the rest from being read. It also coerces the response column to character for every result. This step is important because the consent screen records the button pressed as a number, whereas learning trials record the chosen outcome as text. Consequently, without the coercion, a participant who declined consent would have a numeric response column that cannot be joined to everyone else’s data.

# `parse_jatos_results()` in a single line adds columns `id` (the JATOS result
# ID as text), `jspsych` (one data frame of trials per result, `NULL` when
# nothing could have been parsed), and `has_data` (logical indicating whether
# anything was parsed), keeping the JATOS metadata columns such as `batch_id`
# and `start_date_sr`
results <- parse_jatos_results(jatos_data)

# Next, we manually unroll the `jspsych` data frames, creating a long-format
# table with one row per recorded trial of each participant
jspsych <-
  results |>
  filter(has_data) |>
  select(id, jspsych) |>
  unnest(jspsych)

Results without parseable data remain in results, so that section 6 can exclude them explicitly and the final data bundle records them honestly. However, they are absent from jspsych, the long-format table built above, because they have no trials to unroll.

count(results, batch_id, has_data)
nrow(results)
nrow(jspsych)

3. Provenance

catlasr is designed with the goal of ensuring transparency in the processes behind CATLAS studies in mind. The provenance feature of CATLAS data is one of the tools for making researchers catalogue their data and data-sampling process thoroughly.

The provenance record serves to document what study the data come from, as well as when and how they were collected. This is done via the build_provenance() function, which takes in the following parameters:

Variable type Parameter(s) Use case
Study identifiers study, design CATLAS study ID and design options mapping. Both are more closely discussed in the documentation, see help("build_provenance").
Procedure variables blocks, trial_types State how many blocks of each stage participants were asked to complete and how many trial types each block contains.
Data-sampling platform origin Lists data collection platform as well as a custom study_id, and the batch_ids, if applicable.
Timing variables collected_between, retrieved_at State when the participants underwent the task and when the data were imported to CATLAS.
Experiment specification experiment_build Links to the software code used to create the experiment.
Other things notes, guided notes is there for anything worth knowing about the data that fits no other field; guided = TRUE builds the record interactively in the R console instead of filling it in manually in a script. 
# Timing variables can be derived from the data themselves: the collection
# window from the start times JATOS recorded, the retrieval time from the moment
# `pull_jatos_batches()` finished
collected_between <- c(
  first = as.Date(min(results$start_date_sr, na.rm = TRUE), tz = "Europe/Prague"),
  last  = as.Date(max(results$start_date_sr, na.rm = TRUE), tz = "Europe/Prague")
)
retrieved_at <- attr(jatos_data, "retrieved_at")

# NOTE: Writing CATLAS data provenance correctly is one of the most important
# data import steps. Not only is it the point at which the researcher documents
# the origins of their data, the data bundle-building functions will also not
# work unless they receive a valid `catlas_provenance` object.
prov <- build_provenance(
  study = "fba-allergy-online-01",
  design = "three-stage-replication",
  blocks = c(
    stage1 = 10L,
    stage2 = 8L,
    stage3 = 6L,
    test = 6L
  ),
  trial_types = 8L,
  origin = list(
    platform = "JATOS",
    url = jatos_url,
    study_id = study_id,
    batch_ids = batch_ids
  ),
  collected_between = collected_between,
  retrieved_at = retrieved_at,
  experiment_build = list(
    repo = "josefmana/catlaslab",
    release = "fba-allergy-online-01",
    commit = NA_character_
  ),
  notes = paste(
    "A small number of early runs (all in the 30206 batch) used the experiment",
    "build preceding the 10 June 2026 debriefing patch, which renamed",
    "debriefing variables only. Experimental trials are identical in both",
    "builds. All runs are thus treated alike. The self-reported sex and age",
    "of two participants of the 30206 batch were replaced with their true",
    "values, known to the experimenter, which are kept in the private folder."
  )
)

prov

You may notice that the object states that no exclusion rules were applied yet. Indeed, we have only prepared a provenance record, without attaching it to any data. Once the data bundle is created, we can start excluding records that do not meet inclusion criteria, while appending the reasons to the data bundle provenance record.

4. Data bundle components

A catlas_fba_rawdata bundle has three components, all keyed by the participant identifier id. They are:

Component Content
meta Metadata including participants’ demographic characteristics and experiment set-up, optionally browser and computer variables if run online. Must not contain any e-mail fields.
stimuli Participant-wise mapping of the concrete stimuli to their abstract representations in the study design.
trials Single-trial response data.

Participant metadata

Contains one row per JATOS study record, including records that will be excluded. This is done deliberately, so that every exclusion can be documented with a reference to a known participant/record. Screen and browser details come from the jsPsych browser check, while sex and age come from the demography form. The duration of the run is calculated from the start and end times JATOS recorded, and only for finished runs, because JATOS does not record a reliable end for the rest. Prior knowledge comes from the debriefing question asking whether the participant had taken part in a similar experiment before. The free-text comment of the debriefing is not imported, as it may contain anything, including contact details. The e-mail address collected by the experiment is intentionally dropped, and build_fba_rawdata() refuses any bundle that includes e-mail fields to prevent personal data being pushed to a public repository.

meta_cols <- c(
  "sex", "age",                                                        # Demographics
  "width", "height", "browser", "browser_version", "os", "vsync_rate"  # Browser data
)

meta <-
  results |>
  mutate(
    duration_min = if_else(
      study_state == "FINISHED",
      as.numeric(difftime(end_date_sr, start_date_sr, units = "mins")),
      NA_real_
    )
  ) |>
  select(
    id,           # For cross-reference across data-bundle components
    batch_id,     # For cross-reference with the provenance record
    duration_min  # For the feasibility audit
  ) |>
  left_join(
    jspsych |>
      select(id, all_of(meta_cols)) |>
      summarise(across(everything(), \(x) first(na.omit(x))), .by = id),
    by = "id"
  ) |>
  left_join(
    jspsych |>
      filter(trial_type == "debrief") |>
      select(id, any_of("prior_knowledge")) |>
      summarise(prior_knowledge = as.logical(first(na.omit(prior_knowledge))), .by = id),
    by = "id"
  ) |>
  mutate(age = as.numeric(age)) # The demography form returns age as character

# Count the records in each batch and the records missing `age`. `n` is an upper
# bound on the number of participants, because one person could have run the
# experiment more than once and some records will fail the inclusion criteria.
# `missing_age` counts records that most likely ended before the experimental
# task, since the demography form precedes it.
meta_summary <- summarise(
  meta,
  n = n(),
  missing_age = sum(is.na(age)),
  .by = batch_id
)

meta_summary

Corrected self-reports

Two participants of the 30206 batch, both from the experimenter’s family, entered an untrue sex or age in the demography form. Since the experimenter knows their true values, the code below replace the self-reports. The corrections comprise personal data and therefore live in the private folder, keyed by participant ID, not in this vignette. rows_update() aborts if a corrected ID is not in meta, so a stale correction cannot pass silently. The counts above describe the records as collected, before this correction.

meta <- rows_update(
  meta,
  read_private_rds("fba-allergy-online-01/meta-corrections.rds"),
  by = "id"
)

Stimulus mappings

Every participant saw the abstract cues (A to Z, alpha, beta) and outcomes (o1 to o4) as randomly assigned chemical names and side effects, respectively. The experiment saves this assignment at the start as two JSON strings. In the three-stage-replication study design, outcome images are named <context>_<side effect>, with context referring to one of two imaginary patients and side effect representing the outcome value. Each outcome thus gets two columns in the stimuli component, one for its side effect only (o1 to o4) and one for the patient/context it belongs to (o1_context to o4_context)

# In the `three-stage-*` forward blocking paradigm, cues are represented by
# letters and outcomes by numbers prefixed by a lowercase "o".
cue_labels <- c(LETTERS, "alpha", "beta")
outcome_labels <- paste0("o", 1:4)

stimuli <-
  jspsych |>
  filter(trial_type == "stimuli-map") |> # The trial containing a random participant-specific mapping
  mutate(map = map2(cueMap, outcomeMap, function(cues, outcomes) {
    bind_cols(
      tibble::as_tibble(jsonlite::fromJSON(cues)),
      tibble::as_tibble(jsonlite::fromJSON(outcomes))
    )
  })) |>
  select(id, map) |>
  unnest(map) |>
  select(
    id,
    all_of(cue_labels),
    all_of(outcome_labels)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    across(all_of(outcome_labels), \(x) sub("_.*$", "", x), .names = "{.col}_context"),
    across(all_of(outcome_labels), \(x) sub("^.*_", "", x))
  )

head(stimuli, 5L)

Apart from linking concrete stimuli to their abstract roles in the experiment, e.g., for use in hierarchical modelling accounting for stimulus effects (although these should be taken care of by randomisation), the stimuli component can be used to check how well randomised the stimulus-role pairing ended up.

Trials

During the experiment, the cues of each trial are recorded as a single string, with the cue labels in the order they appeared on the screen, from left to right. fba_cues_map() function exists to turn this string into the cue pair in its canonical order, i.e., cue1 and cue2. It records separately whether the cue pair was shown in reversed order or not. Both presentation orders of a pair therefore land on the same cue1 and cue2 values, while a single cue trial records cue2 and the order variable as NAs:

# This code runs even without the data, so it names its packages explicitly:
catlasr::fba_cues_map("three-stage-replication") |>
  dplyr::filter(label %in% c("A", "AB", "BA"))
#> # A tibble: 3 × 4
#>   label cue1  cue2  cues_reversed
#>   <chr> <chr> <chr> <lgl>        
#> 1 A     A     NA    NA           
#> 2 AB    A     B     FALSE        
#> 3 BA    A     B     TRUE
# NOTE: It makes a lot of sense to provide provenance-recorded design to the
# `fba_cues_map()` function rather than writing it down manually to ensure
# smooth compatibility.
cues_map <- fba_cues_map(prov$design)
trial_cols <- c(
  "stage", "block", "type", "cues",        # Experiment design
  "response", "is_correct", "confidence",  # Primary outcomes
  "rt1", "rt2", "timed_out"                # Time variables
)

trials <-
  jspsych |>
  filter(trial_type == "experiment-trial") |> # The experiment labels its trial via a handy custom jsPsych type
  select(
    id,
    all_of(trial_cols)
  ) |>
  left_join(
    cues_map,
    by = c("cues" = "label")
  )
# Before building the data bundle, let's shuffle columns into their canonical
# order, dropping the `cues` string in the process, as it is fully determined by
# `cue1`, `cue2` and `cues_reversed`.
trials <-
  trials |>
  relocate(cue1, cue2, cues_reversed, .after = type) |>
  select(-cues)

# Let us also inspect the first trial of each stage:
trials |>
  group_by(stage) |>
  slice(1L) |>
  ungroup()

The trials component of the data bundle contains the experiment proper, i.e., the data the study was designed to collect and analyse. In this study, trials contain four main types of rows, one for each stage of the experiment:

  • stage1
    trials contain a single cue (cue1) and a single response (response),
  • stage2
    trials add a second cue (cue2) with left-right counterbalancing indicated by the cues_reversed variable,
  • stage3
    trials copy stage2 formally, but change the context (patient) of the outcome options as well as the options themselves (evident as change from o1, o2 to o3, o4 options in response),
  • test
    trials contain compound cues and add confidence ratings on top of the two-alternative forced choice decision (yielding non-NA confidence and rt2 records)3.

5. Build

With all three components and the provenance record at hand, we can proceed to building the CATLAS data bundle itself. build_fba_rawdata() constructs the bundle and validates it. Structural problems abort the process outright, while anything suspicious that might just be a property of a participant warns, naming the participants concerned.

fba <- build_fba_rawdata(
  meta       = meta,
  stimuli    = stimuli,
  trials     = trials,
  provenance = prov
)

fba

# The object is kept as imported, before any exclusion, so that the later
# feasibility audit can see where the excluded participants stopped
fba_imported <- fba

The console record above shows several warning messages. At this point of the data bundle-building process, the warnings are expected. They list the records without data, the participants who stopped early, and so on. These are then turned into recorded exclusions in section 6.

6. Structural exclusions

In this section, we apply three exclusion rules and implement them using the record_exclusion() function, which applies the criteria, documents the reasons, and appends them to the data bundle’s provenance record.

The rules listed here are ordered by how early in a run they apply and executed in that order. A participant is counted under the first rule that removes them.

No jsPsych data

Some JATOS study results may be empty, i.e., containing no jsPsych data at all. Such records represent artefacts that are not relevant for the study in question.

fba <- record_exclusion(
  fba,
  rule = "no_jspsych_data",
  description = paste(
    "The JATOS study result holds no jsPsych data that can be parsed, for",
    "instance because the study link was opened but no trial record reached",
    "the server."
  ),
  ids = results$id[!results$has_data]
)

Declined to participate

Participants who declined consent still left records on JATOS from the screens preceding the consent form, such as the cue and outcome randomisation map. Consequently, their records need to be excluded before any further processing.

# The consent form records decline to participate as `response` of `"0"`
declined <- unique(jspsych$id[jspsych$trial_type == "consent" & jspsych$response %in% "0"])

fba <- record_exclusion(
  fba,
  rule = "declined_consent",
  description = paste(
    "The participant declined on the informed-consent screen, which ends the",
    "experiment before the first learning trial."
  ),
  ids = declined
)

Incomplete run

To allow for a valid analysis of blocking indices that constitute the primary endpoints of the study, at least one test block must be present in the data. At this point in the workflow, participants with missing learning-trial records who underwent and recorded at least one test block are retained, as their data still allow for primary endpoints calculation.

# The number of distinct trial types per block can and should be extracted from
# provenance at this stage:
n_types <- provenance(fba)$trial_types

completed_test_trials <-
  extract_meta(fba) |>
  select(id) |>
  left_join(
    extract_trials(fba) |>
      summarise(
        n = sum(stage == "test"),
        .by = id
      ),
    by = "id"
  ) |>
  mutate(n = coalesce(n, 0L)) # Test trials missing altogether recorded as `NA` should be treated as zeroes

fba <- record_exclusion(
  fba,
  rule = "incomplete_run",
  description = sprintf(
    "The run does not contain at least one complete test block of %d trials.",
    n_types
  ),
  ids = completed_test_trials$id[completed_test_trials$n < n_types]
)

Exclusion records

The provenance record now carries the three rules together with their verbal description and the number of participants each removed:

print(provenance(fba), exclusions = "long")

Data bundle rebuild

Rebuilding the bundle from its components re-runs every check on the remaining data following the exclusions. Warnings that survive this step are no longer simply informing about incomplete runs and are worth reading closely.

fba <- build_fba_rawdata(
  meta = extract_meta(fba),
  stimuli = extract_stimuli(fba),
  trials = extract_trials(fba),
  provenance = provenance(fba)
)

fba

# These data comprise the full sample, i.e., every participant with a complete
# run, before applying any rule that depends on their responses
fba_structural <- fba

7. Learning-based exclusions

In theory, blocking can only be measured in participants who learned the contingencies of all three learning stages. Consequently, the last exclusion rule removes participants whose learning cannot be reliably told apart from guessing. The functions via which learning-based exclusion is computed use learning stages data only, they do not peek at the test-stage data, keeping the rule blind to the outcome of the study.

The rule takes three deliberate, consecutive steps:

  • score_learning() counts the answered and correct trials per participant, stage, contingency type and block.
  • test_learning() then asks, for every participant and stage, whether there were more correct responses than what guessing would plausibly produce (a one-sided exact binomial test against 0.5), and reports the cut-off, i.e., the smallest number of correct responses at which guessing is rejected.
  • Finally, screen_learning() marks for exclusion every participant who, in one or more stages, did not score significantly above chance, and says why.

All three functions are intentionally talkative; they state their assumptions and summarise the process, so that the user does not take their results as is, but is rather reminded about their potential shortcomings:

learning_alpha  <- 0.10
learning_scores <- score_learning(fba)
learning_tests  <- test_learning(learning_scores, alpha = learning_alpha)
learning_screen <- screen_learning(learning_tests, rule = "any")

learning_screen |>
  filter(exclude) |>
  select(id, failed_stages, reason)

At alpha = 0.10, the Stage 3 cut-off roughly equals the 60% criterion used in the literature. A participant who guesses throughout the full experiment passes all three stages with a probability below 0.001 (help("test_learning") explains the choice more thoroughly).

Here, the rule’s description is built from the same alpha and from the design recorded in provenance, so that the sentence in the provenance record and the rule that was applied cannot disagree:

stages  <- c("stage1", "stage2", "stage3")
n_stage <- provenance(fba)$blocks[stages] * provenance(fba)$trial_types
k_stage <- stats::qbinom(1 - learning_alpha, n_stage, 0.5) + 1

fba <- record_exclusion(
  fba,
  rule = "learning_not_reliably_above_chance",
  description = sprintf(
    paste(
      "The participant did not score significantly above chance in at least",
      "one of the three learning stages, as decided by a one-sided exact",
      "binomial test of the number of correct responses against 0.5 at alpha =",
      "%.2f over all answered trials of the stage (timed-out trials excluded).",
      "On complete data, fewer than %d of %d correct in Stage 1, %d of %d in",
      "Stage 2, or %d of %d in Stage 3. A stage without any answered trial",
      "counts as failed."
    ),
    learning_alpha,
    k_stage[1], n_stage[1],
    k_stage[2], n_stage[2],
    k_stage[3], n_stage[3]
  ),
  ids = learning_screen$id[learning_screen$exclude]
)

fba <- build_fba_rawdata(
  meta = extract_meta(fba),
  stimuli = extract_stimuli(fba),
  trials = extract_trials(fba),
  provenance = provenance(fba)
)

provenance(fba)

# The final dataset for the primary analysis
fba_screened <- fba

The participants removed here stay in fba_structural, which the analysis uses as its full-sample sensitivity check.

8. Prior-knowledge exclusion

Participants who already know a design like this one may answer the test according to what they expect the study to show rather than to what they learned. The debriefing therefore asks whether the participant has taken part in a similar experiment before, and the last rule removes everyone who answered yes. The answer is compulsory in the experiment, so no participant with a complete run lacks it. Like the learning-based rule, this one never looks at the test-stage data.

fba <- record_exclusion(
  fba,
  rule = "prior_knowledge_reported",
  description = paste(
    "The participant answered positiviely to the debriefing question asking",
    "whether they had taken part in a similar experiment before."
  ),
  ids = extract_meta(fba)$id[extract_meta(fba)$prior_knowledge %in% TRUE]
)

fba <- build_fba_rawdata(
  meta = extract_meta(fba),
  stimuli = extract_stimuli(fba),
  trials = extract_trials(fba),
  provenance = provenance(fba)
)

provenance(fba)

# The naive set: the primary set without participants reporting prior knowledge
fba_naive <- fba

9. Save

With the import finished, four bundles can be saved for use by other code, such as the CATLAS notebooks, into the study folder fba-allergy-online-01 of the private folder:

File Bundle Use
fba-allergy-online-01/imported.rds before any exclusion attrition and feasibility
fba-allergy-online-01/structural.rds after the structural exclusions full-sample sensitivity analysis
fba-allergy-online-01/screened.rds after the learning-based exclusions primary analysis
fba-allergy-online-01/naive.rds after the prior-knowledge exclusion naive-set sensitivity analysis 
write_private_rds(fba_imported,   "fba-allergy-online-01/imported.rds",   overwrite = TRUE)
write_private_rds(fba_structural, "fba-allergy-online-01/structural.rds", overwrite = TRUE)
write_private_rds(fba_screened,   "fba-allergy-online-01/screened.rds",   overwrite = TRUE)
write_private_rds(fba_naive,      "fba-allergy-online-01/naive.rds",      overwrite = TRUE)
